claims.text: Machine-learning optimization of processing parameters can enable controlled formation of dual-phase microstructures in metallic alloys.
Controlled dual-phase microstructures can concurrently improve alloy strength and ductility.
Traditionally homogeneous single-phase metallic alloys typically exhibit a trade-off between strength and ductility.
Historical experimental data and microstructural descriptors can be integrated into a machine-learning algorithm to optimize alloy processing.
Data-driven and multi-objective computational strategies can assist alloy design and exploration of composition and temperature effects on microstructure.
Machine-learning optimization can fine-tune heat-treatment and deformation schedules to promote dual-phase or heterogeneous microstructures.
The proposed microstructure comprises a hard phase that provides strength and a more ductile phase that accommodates plastic deformation.
Optimized processing parameters induce controlled phase separation or precipitation.
The hard phase strengthens the alloy by impeding dislocation motion.
The ductile phase sustains plasticity by facilitating dislocation transmission.
A machine-learning model can identify non-intuitive processing windows that reconcile the strength–ductility trade-off.
Machine-learning-guided processing will produce significant concurrent improvements in strength and ductility relative to conventional processing that yields homogeneous microstructures.
Traditional thermomechanical processing typically produces either high strength at the expense of ductility or high ductility at the expense of strength.
The approach is primarily applicable within compositional and processing regimes similar to the machine-learning training data.
The approach may be less effective under extreme processing conditions or for markedly different alloy chemistries.
The magnitudes of the strength and ductility gains depend on the alloy system and the processing window.
Comparing identical alloy samples processed conventionally and with machine-learning-selected parameters can test the hypothesis.
